1902 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON CIRCUITS AND SYSTEMS—II: EXPRESS BRIEFS, VOL. 72, NO. 12, DECEMBER 2025
SVG Conﬁguration Scheme to Enhance Renewable
Energy Accommodation Considering V oltage
Stability Constraints in Renewable Power Grids
Wenshuang Liu, Student Member, IEEE, Jie Yang, Student Member, IEEE, Xi Zhang , Member, IEEE,
Kui Luo, Member, IEEE, Tiezhu Wang , Member, IEEE, Shicong Ma , Member, IEEE, and Liangyi Zhang
Abstract—This brief proposes an effective Static Var Generator
(SVG) conﬁguration scheme to enhance renewable energy
accommodation while considering cost efﬁciency and voltage
stability constraints. First, the multiple renewable short-circuit
ratio (MRSCR) is employed as a voltage stability indicator,
providing a computationally efﬁcient representation of voltage
stability constraints. Subsequently, a double-loop multi-objective
optimization framework is developed to generate an optimal SVG
conﬁguration scheme. The hierarchical structure consists of: (1)
an inner-loop optimal power dispatch model that determines the
minimum curtailment of renewable energy under both voltage
stability constraints and the SVG conﬁguration provided by
the outer loop; (2) an outer-loop multi-objective optimization
model that simultaneously minimizes SVG conﬁguration costs
and annual renewable energy curtailment to establish the
SVG conﬁguration. Experimental validation on the SG-118 test
system demonstrates the superiority of the proposed framework.
Through a comparative analysis of MRSCR characteristics and
renewable energy accommodation levels, this brief presents
an innovative SVG conﬁguration methodology that effectively
balances voltage stability maintenance with renewable energy
integration enhancement.
Index Terms —Static var generator conﬁguration, MRSCR,
renewable energy accommodation, voltage stability, double-loop
multi-objective optimization.
I. I NTRODUCTION
U
NDER the dual imperatives of environmental sustainabil-
ity and low-carbon transition, power systems worldwide
have witnessed rapid integration of renewable energy (RE) such
as photovoltaics (PVs) and wind turbines. While these resources
reduce carbon emissions, their inherent intermittency and lack
of traditional grid-support functionalities introduce critical
challenges to power balance and system stability [1], [2], [3].
These limitations often exacerbate RE curtailment.

To address RE integration barriers, planning strategies such
as large-scale energy storage deployment and coal-ﬁred power
plant ﬂexibility retroﬁts have been widely proposed, primarily
targeting intermittency mitigation [4], [5]. However, a less
apparent yet increasingly critical constraint lies in the voltage
stability of modern power systems–the ability to maintain
acceptable voltage levels across all nodes under normal and
disturbed conditions. RE-dominated power systems inherently
lack the short-circuit capacity and dynamic voltage support
provided by synchronous generators, increasing susceptibility
to voltage instability [6]. V oltage stability manifests in two
forms: static stability and transient stability (overvoltage trig-
gered by faults).
In practice, reactive power compensation devices, such
as Static Var Compensator (SVC), Static Synchronous
Compensator (STATCOM), Synchronous Condenser(SC), etc,
have been used to regulate voltage magnitudes and enhance
grid strength by dynamically injecting or absorbing reac-
tive power. Existing research investigated the placement and
sizing of reactive power compensation devices to ensure
dynamic voltage support during faults by integrating tran-
sient overvoltage constraints [7]. Typical approaches include
sensitivity indices, intelligent optimization algorithms [8],
etc. While current SVG conﬁguration frameworks address
voltage stability requirements in operational timescales [9],
they neglect a critical dimension: long-term RE curtailment
reduction. By focusing solely on improving transient sta-
bility for a speciﬁc operation condition, these models fail
to account for RE output variations and long-term beneﬁts,
such as minimized annual RE curtailment. This oversight
leads to suboptimal planning outcomes where SVG invest-
ments prioritize immediate stability over sustained renewable
utilization.
Due to the complex dynamics and nonlinear interdepen-
dencies between grid topology, renewable generation, and
loads, accurately as well as simply quantifying voltage stability
in power systems is inherently complex. The Short-Circuit
Ratio (SCR) remains a cornerstone metric for evaluating
system strength and voltage stability in numerous relevant
studies [10]. Recent advancements extend SCR formula-
tions to address modern grid challenges, such as high
penetrations of RE and hybrid AC/DC networks, yielding
methods like generalized short-circuit ratio for overvoltage
(gSCR-TOV) [11], generalized short circuit ratio (gSCR) for
multi-infeed system [12], Site-Dependent SCR (SDSCR) [13],
etc. Speciﬁcally, Yu et al. [14] demonstrated that the Multiple

Renewable SCR (MRSCR)—a weighted aggregation of indi-
vidual renewable plant SCRs—effectively captures voltage
sensitivity to power ﬂuctuations in weak grids dominated by
inverter-based resources. Similar to reactive power compensa-
tion device conﬁgurations, a critical gap persists in long-term
planning studies, though MRSCR has been applied to short-
term operational frameworks like voltage security-constrained
unit commitment [15].
In this brief, we propose a double-loop multi-objective
optimization framework for conﬁguring Static Var Generators
(SVGs) in renewable power systems to address the coupled
challenges of voltage instability and RE curtailment in power
systems. Section II establishes the foundational analysis for
representing voltage stability constraints. Building on this,
Section III introduces the double-loop optimization frame-
work. The outer loop formulates a multi-objective optimization
problem to minimize SVG conﬁguration costs and annual RE
curtailment, while the inner loop solves a stochastic planning-
scheduling problem that enforces MRSCR constraints under
varying renewable generation scenarios. To validate the frame-
work, Section IV presents a comprehensive case study on the
SG118 test system. These outcomes underscore the frame-
work’s ability to simultaneously ensure grid stability and
maximize renewable utilization, offering a practical pathway
for high-penetration renewable integration.
II. R
EPRESENTATION OF VOLTAGE
STABILITY CONSTRAINTS
This section elaborates on the critical role of MRSCR in
characterizing voltage stability constraints.
A. Voltage Stability Indicator
V oltage stability has emerged as a critical challenge in
power systems, signiﬁcantly constraining the integration of
RE. Its representation, however, is inherently complex and
computationally intensive. While extensive research has val-
idated the feasibility of modeling static voltage stability,
accurately characterizing transient voltage stability remains a
signiﬁcant challenge due to its highly dynamic and nonlinear
nature.
MRSCR, deﬁned as the ratio of a renewable node’s three-
phase short-circuit capacity to its equivalent nodal power,
serves as a robust indicator of system strength and voltage sta-
bility. This metric effectively captures multi-node interactions,
where higher MRSCR values correlate with stronger system
strength. The MRSCR of RE node i can be expressed as:

enhances MRSCR by reducing the impedance matrix ele-

In conclusion, MRSCR effectively characterizes the voltage
stability constraints of power systems. The reactive power
support capability of SVGs can enhance the MRSCR, thereby
strengthening voltage stability and allowing greater integration
of RE.
III. D
OUBLE -LOOP MULTI -OBJECTIVE OPTIMIZATION
FRAMEWORK
In this section, using voltage stability constraints, we pro-
pose a double-loop multi-objective optimization framework
for conﬁguring SVGs to enhance RE accommodation. As
s h o w ni nF i g .1, the framework comprises two loops: The
outer loop employs a multi-objective optimization model to
minimize SVG conﬁguration costs and annual RE curtailment
while providing conﬁguration parameters for the inner loop;
The inner loop utilizes an optimal power dispatch model to
calculate annual RE curtailment under the outer-loop given
SVG conﬁguration, which directly feeds into the outer-loop
objectives. Specially, after the dispatch result is given by
the inner loop, the objective function 2 of the outer loop
is determined accordingly. Therefore, the outer loop will
optimize the SVG conﬁguration to achieve the minimization
of the RE curtailment in order to minimize the objective
function 2.

B. Effects of the Proposed Method in Enhancing RE
Accommodation
Fig. 3 illustrates the distribution of Pareto front solutions.
Each point represents a unique solution balancing competing
objectives, speciﬁcally the SVG conﬁguration that minimizes
RE curtailment for a ﬁxed number of SVGs. A distinct phase
transition point is observed at 18 SVGs, indicating a signiﬁcant
shift in the trade-off characteristics. This phase transition
point signiﬁes an abrupt change in the system’s behavior as
parameters reach a critical value.

extent with 18 SVGs. This trend highlights the essential role
of SVG conﬁguration in addressing RE variability.
C. Demonstration of Advantages Over Other SVG
Conﬁguration Schemes
We compare annual RE curtailment of our proposed method
with two schemes: one with no SVG and a commonly used
sequential scheme [17]. The sequential scheme deploys SVGs
at nodes with the lowest MRSCR until the predeﬁned limit is
reached, considering only RE nodes as candidates. In contrast,
our optimized conﬁguration scheme includes collection nodes,
which can simultaneously support multiple subordinate RE
nodes. As demonstrated in Fig. 5, our optimized conﬁgura-
tion scheme achieves a signiﬁcant reduction in annual RE
curtailment.

V. C
ONCLUSION
This brief proposes a SVG conﬁguration framework that
maximizes RE accommodation while ensuring voltage sta-
bility at minimal cost. Through a double-loop optimization
framework integrating power dispatch and SVG conﬁguration,
the method determines the most effective SVG conﬁguration
scheme. Simulation results on the SG118 system demonstrate
that the proposed solution signiﬁcantly enhances renewable
utilization without compromising voltage stability, offering
a practical approach for large-scale RE integration. Future
research will include dedicated studies on SVG installation
cost modeling and the characterization of mutual interaction
effects.
